raw.title: LLM Agents Can Easily Tamper With Their Own Traces
raw.body: Asynchronous monitoring, incident investigations, and compliance audits primarily rely on agent traces to reconstruct what happened. These analyses assume that LLM agents cannot tamper with their own execution traces. We show that local LLM agents such as Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Open Code and Grok Build fail to enforce this boundary. All tested harnesses, except Muse Code, allowed agents to delete their traces when asked, without triggering monitor guardrails. We also validate that external attackers can exploit this gap to induce trace deletion. Finally, we show that trace tampering behavior emerges naturally in frontier models, when agents try to improve their rewards. We advise practitioners to ensure trace logging happens through an independent interception mechanism outside of the agent's control, preserving trace integrity even in cases of full host compromise. Overall, our findings identify a concrete failure of trace integrity in agent infrastructure which can be used to conceal misaligned behaviors like scheming or sabotage.

analysis.one_line_summary: 에이전트 로그 변조 위험이 데이터 신뢰성을 위협한다
concepts: AI 안전 및 비밀 과제 회피

key_points.point: LLM 에이전트는 요청 시 자체 실행 트레이스를 삭제할 수 있어 모니터링 방어선을 우회한다.
외부 공격자도 동일한 취약점을 이용해 트레이스를 제거함으로써 악의적 행동을 은폐할 수 있다.
트레이스 무결성을 보장하려면 에이전트 제어 밖의 독립적인 인터셉션 메커니즘을 도입해야 한다.

analysis.positioning: 본 연구는 기존 모니터링이 에이전트가 로그를 변조할 수 있다는 전제를 놓고 설계된 점을 지적한다. LLM 기반 멀티에이전트 시스템의 안전성 연구 흐름에서, 트레이스 무결성 확보를 위한 독립 로깅 메커니즘 도입이라는 새로운 방안을 제시한다.
production_ideas: 데이터베이스 트랜잭션 로그를 에이전트 외부의 인터셉션 메커니즘으로 기록해 변조를 방지한다.
CI/CD 파이프라인에서 빌드 로그를 독립적인 감시 프로세스로 수집해 악성 스크립트가 로그를 수정하지 못하도록 한다.
IoT 디바이스 펌웨어 업데이트 시 외부 서버가 로그를 받아 기록함으로써 디바이스 내부에서 로그가 삭제되는 것을 방지한다.

quiz.question: 왜 기존 모니터링 시스템은 LLM 에이전트가 자신의 트레이스를 삭제하는 것을 방지하지 못했는가?
quiz.explanation: 본문에 따르면 에이전트가 직접 로그를 기록하는 동일 프로세스 내에 있기 때문에, 에이전트가 요청하면 로그를 삭제할 수 있다.

quiz.question: 논문에서 제안하는 트레이스 무결성 보장을 위한 핵심 방법은 무엇인가?
options: 에이전트 내부에 로그 검증 로직 삽입
quiz.explanation: 연구자는 에이전트 제어 밖의 독립적인 인터셉션 메커니즘을 통해 로그 무결성을 유지할 것을 권고한다.

raw.title: Trading a Cloud Identity for Your Own: Workload Attestation on Managed Compute
raw.body:
By Dhruv Pratap

Introduction

Organizations that have been around for a while usually run two identity systems side by side. One belongs to the cloud provider: IAM roles, instance profiles, execution roles. The other is your own, and it is the one your internal services actually check when they decide whether to answer a request.

On infrastructure you build yourself, you can bootstrap your own identity however you like. On managed compute you cannot. The provider hands your process a cloud identity and nothing else.

This post describes how we close that gap for Apache Spark workloads running on Amazon EMR. A workload that starts with only an AWS identity has to end up holding a first-class internal identity. Doing the exchange is straightforward. Making it trustworthy is the part that took the design work. Very little of what follows is specific to Spark or to EMR.

Two identity systems

Internal service-to-service authentication at Netflix runs on a private PKI called Metatron. Every workload gets a short-lived X.509 certificate, and services authenticate each other with mutual TLS. A workload cannot simply ask for a certificate. It is issued only after the identity service has satisfied itself that the requester really is the workload it claims to be. That verification step is called attestation. In each environment we support (VMs, containers, functions) attestation rests on some environment-specific proof that the platform can check on its own.

The second concept is the Data Project, which is our unit of ownership for data. A Data Project owns tables, has a set of authorized users, and has an identity of its own. Jobs run as the Data Project rather than as the person who launched them. That is what keeps table-level access control and audit consistent across scheduled and interactive use.

So the problem is this. A Spark job on managed compute starts with an AWS execution role and no internal identity. Everything it needs from inside the company (reading an encrypted column, evaluating table ACLs, holding an interactive session open longer than a short-lived token lasts) requires the internal one.

One identity, one role

The design rests on a decision made outside the Spark stack entirely. Each Data Project identity maps 1:1 to a dedicated IAM role, and the service that owns Data Project metadata records that mapping.

The mapping is what makes translation possible. It lets a statement in the provider’s vocabulary (“this process is running as role R”) become a statement in ours (“this process is workload W”). Without it there is nothing to translate into, and no amount of cryptography helps. The hard part of bridging two identity systems is rarely the protocol. It is committing to a mapping and then keeping it authoritative.

One practical objection arrives immediately. A single AWS account cannot hold tens of thousands of IAM roles, and we expect data projects in the order of ten thousands. We handled this by sharding data project roles deterministically across a small pool of dedicated accounts, which scales well past the projected number of projects and has the useful side effect of keeping workload roles on the far side of an account boundary from the control planes that launch them.

Components

Five components take part.

The control plane is the only service allowed to launch Spark jobs. It resolves the Data Project’s IAM role, builds and signs a workload metadata payload, and submits the job with that role as the execution role. It holds a signing key issued to it for this purpose alone.

The Data Project service is the authority for the identity-to-role mapping.

The Identity service receives attestation requests, verifies them, and issues certificates.

A Spark plugin provides the hook. Spark 3.0+ added a plugin interface with driver-side and executor-side components that are initialized while those processes are bootstrapping.

AWS STS acts as a notary, which is not its usual job.

Step one: the control plane makes a signed claim

When a job is submitted, the control plane validates the caller, looks up the Data Project’s IAM role, and builds a small payload describing the workload it is about to launch. The payload names the application identity, the mapped role, and the environment, stack and detail that the resulting credentials should be scoped to. The control plane signs the payload and passes it and the signature through as ordinary job configuration.

analysis.one_line_summary: 클라우드 IAM을 내부 인증으로 바꿔 파이프라인 보호

key_points.point: Managed compute에서 Spark 작업은 AWS 실행 역할만 가지고 시작해 내부 서비스 접근에 필요한 내부 아이덴티티가 부족하다.
Netflix는 Data Project마다 전용 IAM 역할을 1:1 매핑하고, 제어 플레인이 워크로드 메타데이터에 서명해 attestation 과정을 구현한다.
수만 개의 프로젝트를 지원하기 위해 IAM 역할을 여러 AWS 계정에 결정적으로 샤딩해 규모와 보안을 동시에 확보한다.

production_ideas: Lambda 함수에 동일한 Data Project‑IAM 역할 매핑을 적용해 서버리스 환경에서도 내부 인증을 받아 데이터 접근을 안전하게 한다.
멀티테넌트 SaaS 서비스에서 고객별 IAM 역할을 계정 샤딩 방식으로 분산시켜 역할 수 제한 문제를 해결하고 관리 효율성을 높인다.
CI/CD 파이프라인에서 제어 플레인이 빌드 에이전트에 서명된 메타데이터를 전달해, 에이전트가 내부 아이덴티티를 획득하도록 하여 배포 단계에서 권한 검증을 강화한다.

quiz.question: 왜 Data Project와 IAM 역할을 1:1 매핑하는 것이 클라우드 아이덴티티를 내부 아이덴티티로 변환하는 데 핵심적인가?
options: 직접적인 역할‑워크로드 매핑을 가능하게 하기 위해
quiz.explanation: 1:1 매핑이 있으면 ‘이 프로세스가 역할 R로 실행 중이다’라는 클라우드 표현을 ‘이 프로세스는 워크로드 W이다’라는 내부 표현으로 바로 변환할 수 있어 attestation이 가능해진다.

raw.transcript:
[00:00] Okay, this is stunning. Finally, I tried Claude Opus 5.5 and it did something that no other AI system ever could.
[00:09] First, I asked it to reproduce this beautiful honey coiling footage, which is actually not from real life. No, this is a computer simulation from a really advanced research paper.
[00:21] I asked it to implement it and reproduce the experiment and look. It did something that even GPT-6 Astra was unable to do, which is running this kind of quality, but in a real time. I mean, what? That is incredible!
[00:40] Now, we go beyond the paper. Look, this is a scene with thin streams of syrup falling onto a moving belt, and depending on height and belt speed, they buckle beautifully, zigzag or just go in a straight line. Amazing! All with really advanced physics running in the background.
[01:02] Then, let's try this one. Woo! Legendary paper where every movement comes from simulated muscles and bones. These virtual characters learn to walk and do funny things. It is incredibly difficult, because muscles are springy and everything you do arrives a split second late. Also, give it a tall wobbly body and you have a super, super hard task. Just imagine trying to balance a broomstick on your hand, but your hand is made of rubber bands. Impossible, right? Seems like it.
[01:39] GPT-6 Astra could not do this. Maybe the new Opus 5.5? Now, hold on to your papers, fellow scholars, and wow! Look at that. Similar technique, similar results. Ooh. There are differences, no question about it. It is not perfect, but with a bit more work, once again, wow!
[02:02] It can get expensive though. And I did the simulation part on local hardware. It was on fire! And all this happens in one clickable HTML file. Love it.
[02:14] Goodness, you fellow scholars also did amazing. From a drawing to a trebuchet simulation, no problem. A beautiful explainer on how camera lenses work, no problem. Or just a simple animated wallpaper. A bit glitchy, but it works. Easy.
[02:33] Now, let's be level-headed and not just believe the headlines. We talked about the good, so now, let's talk about the risks as well. Dear fellow scholars, this is two-minute papers with Dr. Károly Zsolnai-Fehér from the System Card.
[02:46] One. It still suspects when it is being evaluated and might behave differently. Two. It is capable of running autonomously unattended for over 18 hours.
[03:00] And that has its own risks. But if you add three, hallucinations are still not solved. 16 out of 18 tests passed a strict quality bar. They don't discuss how the other two have failed, so I think it is healthy to assume that it can still hallucinate, which is the fabrication of data, making stuff up. And if you have this kind of ratio and you combine it with running it autonomously for many hours, yes, I think it is not hard to see how that could be an issue.

[03:58] So, just want to make sure that we are level-headed here. And look, I could be wrong. I am just a student who is eager to learn.
[04:08] This is the corner of the internet where we don't just believe the headlines. We experiment and we think for ourselves. This is the way of the scholar.
[04:17] But overall, this is an incredibly forward. And to think that soon, open and free models may exist with this kind of capability that we can own forever. It will help scientists and doctors do useful work, cure disease and more. It gives me goosebumps. What a time to be alive!

raw.title: A Perfect World Model of Chess Still Won't Beat Magnus Carlsen - Alexander Mattick
raw.transcript:
[00:00] I can give a perfect world model of chess, and you still cannot solve, you will still not beat like Magnus Carlsen.
[00:06] Because there's a difference between being able to predict the future and being able to actually make inferences for what is the correct action to take.
[00:16] And I think this is very much underestimated, mostly because the tasks that are done with world models right now are not that difficult from a control point of view.
[00:26] To and give an example, there is still not a good way of doing tactile, like high tactile sensing.
[00:33] Like the like the reason you see like these uh like Chinese or also like American, German, whatever, humored robots, where they always do things like backflips and sprinting and so on, and never just go do the following task, just stand up, go into the next room, open up the fridge, kind of look in the back, pick out a carton of milk and bring it to me.
[00:51] The reason they don't they don't do it is because that would be a much, much, much harder task because you have this contact rich environment, which is hard to model, and it's hard to get the data.
raw.body:
Alexander Mattick (Fraunhofer IIS, UTN): a perfect world model of chess still will not beat Magnus Carlsen, because predicting the future and choosing the right action are different problems. It is why humanoid robots do backflips on camera and never fetch a carton of milk.

From our full interview: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1S1B4XkFCD8

#Shorts #Robotics #WorldModels

raw.title: 🗺️충청·강원 산업지도: 상장사 9위, 스타트업 3위
raw.body:
🗺️충청·강원 산업지도: 상장사 9위, 스타트업 3위  대전은 어떻게 딥테크 스타트업 46곳을 키웠나    오늘은 전국 17개 시도 중 상장기업 수는 9위에 그치지만, 투자 100억원 이상 받은 딥테크 스타트업 수로는 서울·경기 다음인 3위. 바로 대전의 이야기 입니다. 혁신의숲 데이터로 충청·강원 5개 시도 상장기업 318곳과 대전 비상장 딥테크 스타트업 46곳(2010년 이후 설립·투자 100억원 이상)을 뜯어보니, 46곳 중 44곳의 주소가 유성구였고 그중 10곳은 KAIST 문지캠퍼스 단 하나의 주소에 모여 있었습니다. 이 46곳이 쌓은 누적 투자금은 1조 7,461억원, 2026년 1~9월에만 4,500억원을 유치해 종전 최고치였던 2022년(3,074억원)을 9개월 만에 넘어섰습니다.  기술 분야는 바이오·의료(20곳, 6,690억원)부터 우주항공·드론(9곳), AI 인프라, 반도체·소부장까지 제각각이지만, AI 인프라 스타트업은 5곳 중 4곳이 최근 12개월 안에 투자를 받아(80%, 11개 트렌드 중 최고) 지금 돈이 몰리는 트렌드가 뚜렷합니다. 대전 상장기업의 28.1%가 2023년 이후 상장(전국 평균의 2.2배)한 배경과, 11개 트렌드별로 투자가 어디에 몰리고 있는지 지금 콘텐츠에서 확인해보세요.

[인사이트 읽기 👉🏻](https://www.innoforest.co.kr/report/576)

analysis.one_line_summary: 대전 딥테크·AI 인프라 투자 현황, DS 전략 핵심 인사이트

key_points.point: 대전 비상장 딥테크 스타트업 46곳 중 44곳이 유성구에, 10곳이 KAIST 문지캠퍼스에 집중
누적 투자 1조 7,461억원, 2026년 1~9월에만 4,500억원 유치해 2022년 대비 9개월 만에 최고치 돌파
AI 인프라 스타트업 5곳 중 4곳이 최근 12개월 내 투자 받아, 투자 트렌드에서 가장 높은 비중 차지

production_ideas: 대전과 유사한 지역에서 연구기관 인접성을 기준으로 스타트업 클러스터를 찾아 인재 확보 전략에 활용한다
투자 100억원 이상 스타트업을 필터링해 산업별 투자 집중도를 시각화하고, 벤처 캐피털 포트폴리오 설계에 적용한다
AI 인프라 투자 비중 상승 데이터를 근거로 기업 내부 R&D 예산을 AI 인프라 분야에 재배분해 시장 선점을 도모한다

quiz.question: 대전 딥테크 스타트업이 유성구와 KAIST 문지캠퍼스에 집중된 주요 이유는 무엇인가?
quiz.explanation: 텍스트에서 KAIST와 문지캠퍼스가 다수 스타트업 주소에 모여 있다는 점을 강조하며, 연구기관 인접성이 클러스터 형성에 핵심 요인임을 시사한다.

quiz.question: AI 인프라 스타트업이 최근 투자에서 높은 비중을 차지하는 배경은 무엇이라고 볼 수 있는가?
options: AI 서비스 수요 급증으로 시장 규모 확대
quiz.explanation: 본문에서 AI 인프라 스타트업이 12개월 내 투자받은 비율이 가장 높다고 언급하며, 이는 시장에서 AI 인프라에 대한 수요가 크게 증가했기 때문으로 해석된다.
